description: Hi! I’m Oleksandr an engineer working with satellite communication protocols [e.g., telemetry, ground station links, CCSDS]. We’re tackling the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge: building an intuitive tool that shows when candidate landing sites at the lunar south pole get sunlight for power and line-of-sight to Earth for direct communication.
summary:
Polar Window is a free web app that helps mission planners, teachers and the public find the best place and time to land on the Moon. Pick any of 54 sites, from Artemis III candidate regions to Apollo landings, or type any coordinates. The app shows, hour by hour, the Sun and Earth against that site's real terrain horizon: how much solar power a lander gets, when it can talk directly to Earth, and how long until sunset or Earthset.

When a launch slips, one click shows what each day of delay costs and which nearby sites do better on the same dates. Every mission plan is checked three ways: an exact calculation(rules), our own AI (an LSTM neural network) and SAPLE formal verification.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Polar Window is a free web app for comparing lunar landing sites and dates. Choose one of 54 curated sites (NASA Artemis III candidate regions, CLPS landings such as IM-1, IM-2 and Blue Ghost 1, all six Apollo sites, and other nations' landers) or type any coordinates on the Moon. For that spot, the app shows the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, hour by hour: solar power, energy per day, when the lander can talk directly to Earth, battery reserve through each dark spell, and countdowns to the next sunset and Earthset. When plans change, the Compare tab shows what a launch slip of -3 to +28 days does to the mission, ranks nearby sites within 25-250 km for the same dates, and puts up to three scenarios side by side.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline turns NASA LRO LOLA elevation data into a terrain horizon for every site, with 720 sight lines out to 300 km that include the Moon's curvature. In the browser, astronomy-engine computes Sun and Earth positions using the IAU lunar rotation model; across 216 JPL Horizons reference values they match within 0.002 degrees. Five mission rules (sunlight for the whole stay, battery never empty, Earth comes into view, enough Earth contact, never without both) are checked three ways: an exact hour-by-hour calculation, our own LSTM neural network with attention (trained on 230,850 stays; 99.8% correct on sites it never saw), and SAPLE formal verification (1,350 missions, all matching the exact calculation).

BENEFITS

Questions like "what if we land three days later?" or "is the ridge 4 km away better?" are answered in seconds instead of combining several tools by hand. Example: moving 4.3 km west of the Malapert Massif point lifts average sunlight from 44% to 58%. Everything runs in any browser, with nothing to install, and share links reopen the exact view.

INTENDED IMPACT

Mission planners can screen sites and launch windows quickly before a deeper study. Teachers and students get a Learn mode that explains, with live numbers, why the polar Sun skims the horizon and why Earth can hide behind a ridge. The public can see why landing at the lunar south pole is so hard, and so worth it.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, three.js, Vite and Vitest for the web app; Python with NumPy, SciPy and Pillow for the data pipeline; PyTorch to train the neural network, which then runs in the browser; astronomy-engine for ephemerides; SAPLE ( Z3 solver) for formal verification; GitHub Actions for tests; static hosting on Cloudflare. No special hardware: everything was built and trained on a laptop.

CODE

https://github.com/smander/nasa_phoenix_systems_2026 (with all pipelines) , only SAPLE need to be installed on platform as it system app https://saple.cloud/

CREATIVITY

Each mission is judged three ways: the AI predicts, the exact calculation computes, and formal verification proves. When they disagree, the app says so.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: we validated against JPL Horizons and built tests around it. Honesty: "Earth in view" means line of sight, not a scheduled ground-station pass, and verdicts the public site cannot verify live are labelled "preview". Known limits: 240 m terrain smooths narrow ridge crests, and region coordinates are region centres. Speed: heavy terrain work is done once in advance, so the site stays fast and static. Accessibility: a Learn mode, and status shown in words as well as colour. Data: only NASA open data, with no NASA logos.
